passage:
Mentor's note, Friday. Rashmi here, writing up the five weeks I sat in on Joseph's team.
Tuesday after the first investor chat, Joseph told everyone to add an AI helper. Two weeks later, after another chat, the plan became fast delivery. Last week, after a third, it turned into a marketplace. Each time, half-built work was put aside.
At the Thursday stand-up one engineer said quietly, "We never finish a test before the next idea arrives." Nobody replied, and two people looked at their laptops.
I asked Joseph what the numbers said about any of the three. There were no numbers, because nothing ran long enough to measure. We agreed to talk again on Monday.

qa.q: Which three ideas did the product swing toward?
qa.a: It swung toward an AI helper, fast delivery and a marketplace.

qa.q: What does the engineer's remark at the stand-up suggest about how the team felt?
qa.a: It suggests the engineer felt frustrated and doubtful, because nothing they built stayed around long enough to be tested.

qa.q: What could Joseph do differently with the next idea?
qa.a: Joseph could pick one idea, set a fixed stretch of time and one measure for it, and tell the team before changing course, so the test can finish.

qa.q: Why might Joseph feel each change was sensible at the time?
qa.a: After each investor chat Joseph had just heard fresh interest, so the newest idea would have looked like the safest bet.

grounding: The note shows a founder redirecting the product after each investor conversation so that nothing is tested long enough to learn from.

passage:
Pema's diary, Friday.
Rekha resigned today. She said it kindly: "I don't know what we're building any more."
She's not wrong. In January an investor said everything needs AI, so I made us add an AI study buddy. In March another investor said quick delivery was where the money was, so we started talking to stationery shops about ten-minute delivery. Last month I came back from a coffee and told the team we'd become a marketplace for tutors.
Each time, I was excited. Each time, we dropped the last thing after two or three weeks, before we'd learned whether it worked. The team stopped asking questions in meetings. I thought that meant they agreed.
Now I can't answer one simple question: did any of it work? We never tested anything long enough to know.

qa.q: What did Rekha say when resigning?
qa.a: "I don't know what we're building any more."

qa.q: How does Pema feel looking back on the team going quiet in meetings?
qa.a: Pema feels regretful and a little ashamed, realising the silence was lost trust, not agreement.

qa.q: What would you change first in Pema's approach?
qa.a: Pick one direction and test it for a fixed period with a clear measure, treating investor comments as ideas to check, not orders.

qa.q: What was it like for Rekha during those months?
qa.a: Rekha felt confused and lost, watching the product change every few weeks until the goal was no longer clear.

grounding: It shows a founder swinging the product after each investor chat, from AI to quick delivery to a marketplace, so the team loses trust and nothing is tested long enough.

passage:
Leela: Disha, quick q before standup. are we still doing the marketplace?
Disha: marketplace is paused. after yesterday's investor call I think we go AI-first
Leela: we paused quick delivery 3 weeks ago for the marketplace
Leela: and paused the AI planner in Feb for quick delivery
Disha: I know but the market is moving fast!! we can't miss it
Leela: I get that. but we never got results on any of them. the delivery pilot had 2 weeks. marketplace had 3
Leela: the engineers asked me last night if you'll change it again next week. I didn't know what to say
Disha: 😟
Disha: that's not fair, I'm trying to save the company
Leela: I know you are. but they've stopped believing the plan will last
Leela: can we pick ONE and give it 8 weeks?

qa.q: How long did the marketplace get?
What was Disha feeling when replying "that's not fair"?
qa.a: Disha felt hurt and defensive, believing the changes were an effort to save the company.

qa.q: What does Leela suggest, and why could it work?
qa.a: Picking one idea and giving it eight weeks, long enough to actually learn whether it works.

qa.q: How do the engineers see the constant changes?
qa.a: They have stopped believing the plan will last and are asking whether it will change again next week.

grounding: It shows a founder switching the product toward each fashionable idea after investor calls, so the team loses trust and no idea is tested long enough to learn.
